extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Home » General » Business » Mathematicians claim proof of 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis using AI, human methods New Delhi, Nov 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) Two mathematicians have made competing claims to have solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, setting up a rare contest between an AI-assisted approach and a proof developed through human mathematical reasoning. extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Home » General » Business » Mathematicians claim proof of 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis using AI, human methods New Delhi, Nov 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) Two mathematicians have made competing claims to have solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, setting up a rare contest between an AI-assisted approach and a proof developed through human mathematical reasoning. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, earlier this week said that he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with assistance from Anthropic's Claude AI model. Alessandro Maria Masullo, a researcher at Stanford University, on the same day forwarded a separate proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil described as having been developed without AI assistance. While Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, Masullo’s proof has attracted queries from mathematicians examining the draft. However, the problems reported by several mathematicians were also identified with them using assistance from different AI models. Vakil said the issues would need to be resolved before Masullo’s proof could be accepted. Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing nearly 17.4 million lines of Lean code, a mathematical language used to formalise and verify proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. The Riemann hypothesis was proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, as a mathematical theory on the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain the pattern in which these numbers appear, through a mathematical function, namely, Riemann zeta function. Proving the hypothesis is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. However, a proposed proof must undergo at least two years of scrutiny after appearing in a qualifying peer-reviewed journal. Further, the proof should gain broad acceptance among mathematicians before the prize can be awarded. Gopi Adusumilli is a Programmer. In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis." As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers." As Scientific American notes , the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it. Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes. This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy . Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." "In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds. In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis."

As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers."

As Scientific American notes , the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it.

Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.

This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy .

Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."
"In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.

The proposed proof also addresses the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader version of the original conjecture.The claim has drawn attention from leading mathematicians, although the proof still needs wider independent scrutiny and a deeper understanding of its mathematical reasoning.

extraction.body: An Anthropic mathematician has claimed to have developed a proof of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis with the help of the company's artificial intelligence model Claude, potentially marking a landmark moment for AI-assisted mathematical research.Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced on Friday that he believed he had solved the famous mathematical problem, which concerns the distribution of prime numbers and has remained unresolved since 1859. The proposed proof also addresses the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader version of the original conjecture.The claim has drawn attention from leading mathematicians, although the proof still needs wider independent scrutiny and a deeper understanding of its mathematical reasoning. James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, expressed optimism about the result.“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject,” Maynard told IBM Think in an interview. “This result really stands out, even in the context of all the recent AI breakthroughs.”Alpöge shared the proposed proof in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments step by step. The format allows researchers to examine whether each part of the reasoning follows logically, although verifying the computer-checked argument and understanding the ideas behind it are separate challenges.In a statement posted on his website, Alpöge wrote: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”What is the Riemann hypothesis?First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, which are divisible only by themselves and one. Examples include 2, 3 and 5.Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, the Riemann hypothesis predicts that their distribution follows a deeper mathematical pattern. Each carries a prize of $1 million for a correct solution.Alpöge's announcement follows a series of AI-assisted advances in mathematics, with large language models increasingly being used to explore complex conjectures and theoretical problems. The latest claim, if verified, would represent a major step beyond earlier results that established the predicted pattern for only a proportion of certain mathematical values.Why the proposed proof mattersYouness Lamzouri, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France, said the proposed result would go substantially further than an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough.Previous work had established that at least 67.25% of a particular set of mathematical values followed the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would establish that all of them follow the pattern without exception.Lamzouri, who developed a shorter proof of the earlier result without AI, said the latest announcement had left him astonished.“I don’t have words to describe what I am feeling right now. “If this claim happens to be true, it will be a huge achievement.”However, he cautioned that checking the computer-generated proof would only be the first step. Mathematicians would also need to understand the reasoning and ideas behind it before accepting its broader implications.“Mathematics is mainly about understanding why something is true,” he said. I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.”Sutherland said the achievement should also be viewed in the context of the human work behind the development of Lean, large language models and centuries of mathematical research.“There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he said. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”A turning point for AI-assisted mathematics?Alpöge's claim comes after a year of growing attention on the ability of AI models to tackle difficult mathematical problems. He had earlier attracted attention in July after sharing a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture. He was also involved in a September controversy surrounding an OpenAI mathematical result related to the Navier-Stokes problem.If the Riemann hypothesis proof is independently verified and its reasoning understood, it could mark a major advance in the use of AI for mathematical discovery. The result would not necessarily have immediate practical applications, but it could reshape research in number theory and deepen understanding of connections across mathematics.For now, the central question is whether the proposed proof withstands independent examination. Even if the computer verification holds, mathematicians will need to establish why the argument works and what new avenues it opens.You use AI every day.

passages: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with the help of a large language model.
Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that even a first reading suggested the proof's new ideas could open fresh avenues in number theory.

Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile said a correct and well-understood proof would complete a dictionary between branches of mathematics whose connections were previously partial, something like a Rosetta Stone.
The announcement came on a Friday, a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market.
It has long been the guiding problem of number theory.
The Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize for its solution, and progress was so rare that many leading experts devoted little time to it, since no clear route to a proof existed.
The publication reporting the claim has also carried a follow-up saying independent mathematicians consider the proof almost certainly true, though that report is not reproduced here.
In a statement on his website, he said he believed he had discovered the proof while working with Claude.

He was also central to a September controversy involving OpenAI and the Navier-Stokes problem, in which New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had used his and Alpöge's work improperly.
Many results across mathematics are currently conditional on it, so a proof would immediately turn them into established truths.

passages: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with the help of a large language model.
Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that even a first reading suggested the proof's new ideas could open fresh avenues in number theory.

Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile said a correct and well-understood proof would complete a dictionary between branches of mathematics whose connections were previously partial, something like a Rosetta Stone.
The announcement came on a Friday, a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market.
It has long been the guiding problem of number theory.
The Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize for its solution, and progress was so rare that many leading experts devoted little time to it, since no clear route to a proof existed.
The publication reporting the claim has also carried a follow-up saying independent mathematicians consider the proof almost certainly true, though that report is not reproduced here.
In a statement on his website, he said he believed he had discovered the proof while working with Claude.

He was also central to a September controversy involving OpenAI and the Navier-Stokes problem, in which New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had used his and Alpöge's work improperly.
Many results across mathematics are currently conditional on it, so a proof would immediately turn them into established truths.

Alpöge says his proof establishes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a far broader version of the original conjecture. Errors can still arise in how a statement is encoded in Lean, so experts must confirm that the hypothesis has been formalised correctly and that the proof is sound. Andrew Sutherland of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology said he independently compiled the result in Lean. Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that even a first reading suggested the proof's new ideas could open fresh avenues in number theory. Its importance lies in what it would demonstrate about the intellectual reach of machines. In July, he posted a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture, which began an unusually eventful summer for the discipline. He was also central to a September controversy involving OpenAI and the Navier-Stokes problem, in which New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had used his and Alpöge's work improperly. An earlier breakthrough came in October, when one of the results in a large release of mathematics from OpenAI made notable progress in understanding the primes. The claim follows a year in which AI systems moved from unreliable problem-solvers to tools of exceptional power across the discipline. Alpöge's statement acknowledges the sense of loss many mathematicians feel, yet he describes what he witnessed as the dawn of something far greater across science. Sutherland offered a similar perspective, suggesting the most important step in the proof was the building of a machine capable of thinking. He also credited the human effort behind Lean, language models and the centuries of mathematics on which they rest.

sources.title: Trump downplays breach into FBI’s crime database while reviving complaints about agency’s Russia probe
passages: “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.” The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers, which was first reported by CNN, is the second such breach in recent months, coming as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system.

President Donald Trump on Saturday seemed to downplay a breach into the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, using the incident to revisit his longstanding and unrelated grievances with the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election.

In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.
“I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News when asked about the breach.

During his Fox News interview, Trump implied that the latest breach could uncover information about his 2019 phone call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the president was accused of pressuring Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden, leading to his first impeachment by the House of Representatives.

“We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN.
“I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany.
But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach.

But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach. The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported. In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported. During his Fox News interview, Trump implied that the latest breach could uncover information about his 2019 phone call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the president was accused of pressuring Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden, leading to his first impeachment by the House of Representatives. “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” Trump said, without citing evidence, as he listed “other hoaxes” he said the breach could reveal information about. “I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany. “So as soon as you said that, and as soon as I heard about it a little bit before, I said, ‘Well, that’s an interesting situation. I wonder who’s doing it because wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?’” Trump during his first term repeatedly criticized the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and potential links to his campaign. At one point before the election that year, he encouraged Russian officials accused of hacking into the Democratic National Committee’s computer system to publish any incriminating emails related to his opponent, former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, which they then tried to do, according to a 2018 federal indictment filed against 12 Russian intelligence operatives. The president on Saturday declined to share specific information on the intrusion into the FBI’s system, which serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement.

My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.
A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach.

After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported.

In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported.

“I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany.
“So as soon as you said that, and as soon as I heard about it a little bit before, I said, ‘Well, that’s an interesting situation.

I wonder who’s doing it because wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?’” Trump during his first term repeatedly criticized the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and potential links to his campaign.

At one point before the election that year, he encouraged Russian officials accused of hacking into the Democratic National Committee’s computer system to publish any incriminating emails related to his opponent, former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, which they then tried to do, according to a 2018 federal indictment filed against 12 Russian intelligence operatives.
The president on Saturday declined to share specific information on the intrusion into the FBI’s system, which serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump on Saturday seemed to downplay a breach into the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, using the incident to revisit his longstanding and unrelated grievances with the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News when asked about the breach. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.” The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers, which was first reported by CNN, is the second such breach in recent months, coming as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system. But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach. The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported. In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported. During his Fox News interview, Trump implied that the latest breach could uncover information about his 2019 phone call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the president was accused of pressuring Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden, leading to his first impeachment by the House of Representatives. “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” Trump said, without citing evidence, as he listed “other hoaxes” he said the breach could reveal information about. “I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany. “So as soon as you said that, and as soon as I heard about it a little bit before, I said, ‘Well, that’s an interesting situation. I wonder who’s doing it because wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?’” Trump during his first term repeatedly criticized the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and potential links to his campaign. At one point before the election that year, he encouraged Russian officials accused of hacking into the Democratic National Committee’s computer system to publish any incriminating emails related to his opponent, former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, which they then tried to do, according to a 2018 federal indictment filed against 12 Russian intelligence operatives. The president on Saturday declined to share specific information on the intrusion into the FBI’s system, which serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement.

extraction.body: WASHINGTON — The FBI is investigating an apparent cyberattack against its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a critical law enforcement database, according to news reports Saturday, November 21, 2026. CNN first reported the intrusion, citing people familiar with the investigation. The Associated Press subsequently confirmed the investigation through another source. The FBI declined comment. The hackers’ identities, methods and whether sensitive information was stolen remain unknown. President Donald Trump addressed the incident during a Fox News interview. “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good,” Trump said. However, Trump suggested the breach might expose previously undisclosed information concerning investigations involving Russia, Ukraine and alleged election fraud. The NCIC is a nationwide computerized information-sharing network operated by the FBI. Federal, state and local police use it to identify fugitives, locate missing persons, check arrest warrants, examine criminal histories and identify stolen vehicles, firearms and other property. In November 2025, former Maryland sheriff’s deputy Dontae Odom received a six-month jail sentence for unauthorized searches involving romantic partners and others. In January 2025, former Bryant, Arkansas, officer Christopher Bennett was arrested for illegally accessing the state crime database. extraction.body: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.” The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said. He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom. Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources.

sources.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Called Public Humiliation a ‘Rite of Passage’ For Employees - SFist
passages: The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources.
Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people.
Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits.
Huang reportedly defended the public humiliation as a “rite of passage,” saying he subjected new employees to it during their first six months to see whether they could tolerate it.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.
Despite the accounts of his behavior, Huang also inspired considerable loyalty among Nvidia employees, some of whom have publicly called for his return since his departure.
Thousands reportedly signed a letter asking him to come back, while others have defended his leadership, crediting his technical expertise, vision, and personal support, according to the Times.
Some employees even have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo.
Huang’s treatment of employees reportedly continued as Nvidia grew into a $5 trillion company, per the Times.
In one instance, he publicly mocked an executive who took his children camping, suggesting he needed to find someone more committed to the job.
He also repeatedly made fun of another executive’s interest in aviation.
In 2007, former Nvidia attorney Stephen Pettigrew sued the company, alleging age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s complaints.
He said the company's conduct had caused him to seek emergency medical attention for severe anxiety and nervous tension.
Nvidia denied wrongdoing, countersued over alleged contract violations and misuse of company documents, and settled the case out of court in 2009.

Huang argued that sharing information publicly benefited the entire company, but executives told the Times they viewed the arrangement as a way for Huang to maintain control and make it harder for anyone to challenge him without being publicly ridiculed.

passages: “I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston reportedly wrote in notes at the time, describing Nvidia staff being terrorized by Huang at an Nvidia off-site meeting. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston also said that Huang told him at the time that public humiliation was a “rite of passage.”
The New York Times reports that Huang governed Nvidia through humiliation and terror, frequently attacking employees with bizarre and violent verbal attacks.

These personal attacks often took place in front of other coworkers, and were nothing if not creative: Huang reportedly yelled at one executive that he should’ve been aborted, told another employee that he’d rip off their arms and use them to beat that person to death, and told someone else he would scalp them and “pee on your brain.”
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds a near-mythic status in Silicon Valley as the figurehead of the chipmaker powering the AI boom.
Sources at Nvidia, however, told the NYT that they felt their relationship with Huang was akin to Stockholm Syndrome, wherein people become emotionally attached to their abuser.

A spokesperson for Huang responded to Winston’s allegations, calling them “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” but didn’t respond to other questions about Huang’s aggressive behavior, per the report.

Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds a near-mythic status in Silicon Valley as the figurehead of the chipmaker powering the AI boom. He also, according to new reporting, could be an absolute nightmare as a boss.

The New York Times reports that Huang governed Nvidia through humiliation and terror, frequently attacking employees with bizarre and violent verbal attacks. These personal attacks often took place in front of other coworkers, and were nothing if not creative: Huang reportedly yelled at one executive that he should’ve been aborted, told another employee that he’d rip off their arms and use them to beat that person to death, and told someone else he would scalp them and “pee on your brain.”

Some Nvidia insiders told the NYT that Huang once walked around a room of employees telling them he’d kill them, before stopping in front of an older employee, who was in their 70s, to declare that everyone hoped he’d just die.

The reporting sheds new light on Huang’s stewardship of Nvidia, now the biggest company in the world, as the embattled founder — and the world — grapple with his shocking ouster amid revelations of sex scandal and espionage.

Huang resigned from his role at Nvidia this month after it was revealed that he’d had extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and multiple Nvidia staffers, including a direct report . Seen by many in the tech world as a hero of the AI boom, Huang has received an outpouring of support from across the tech industry — and even from the president of the United States, with whom Huang is close. Thousands of Nvidia staff have signed a petition urging for his reinstatement, as have many tech and business leaders .

Sources at Nvidia, however, told the NYT that they felt their relationship with Huang was akin to Stockholm Syndrome, wherein people become emotionally attached to their abuser. Huang also had a practice of speaking to groups of employees at a time as opposed to holding one-on-ones, which the now-former CEO billed as a way to create transparency — yet others saw as a power play that allowed Huang to berate managers in front of their staff, while also putting employees in a position where, should they want to confront their CEO, they’d have to do with others present.

Huang’s behavior started long before Nvidia became the biggest company in the world, according to the reporting. Back in 2005, a human resources executive named Michael Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment, claiming that he was fired for raising alarms about Huang’s abuse of staffers. Winston also drafted a lawsuit, but the two sides settled before it was ever filed.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston reportedly wrote in notes at the time, describing Nvidia staff being terrorized by Huang at an Nvidia off-site meeting. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston also said that Huang told him at the time that public humiliation was a “rite of passage.”

Nvidia declined to comment on the NYT ’s reporting. A spokesperson for Huang responded to Winston’s allegations, calling them “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” but didn’t respond to other questions about Huang’s aggressive behavior, per the report.

Cruel management styles are common in Silicon Valley. As the NYT points out, the late Apple founder Steve Jobs was also known to blow up at staffers, yet was a beloved leader and and continues to be heralded as a great 21st Century visionary. Elon Musk also has a reputation for being extraordinarily demanding of his workers, expecting them to sleep in factories and offices . Still, “pee on your brain” is a new one.

coreStoryFacts.text: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years.

In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles.
They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said.
The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources.
Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people.
Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits.
Huang reportedly defended the public humiliation as a “rite of passage,” saying he subjected new employees to it during their first six months to see whether they could tolerate it.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.
Despite the accounts of his behavior, Huang also inspired considerable loyalty among Nvidia employees, some of whom have publicly called for his return since his departure.
Thousands reportedly signed a letter asking him to come back, while others have defended his leadership, crediting his technical expertise, vision, and personal support, according to the Times.
Some employees even have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo.
Huang’s treatment of employees reportedly continued as Nvidia grew into a $5 trillion company, per the Times.
In one instance, he publicly mocked an executive who took his children camping, suggesting he needed to find someone more committed to the job.
He also repeatedly made fun of another executive’s interest in aviation.
In 2007, former Nvidia attorney Stephen Pettigrew sued the company, alleging age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s complaints.
He said the company's conduct had caused him to seek emergency medical attention for severe anxiety and nervous tension.
Nvidia denied wrongdoing, countersued over alleged contract violations and misuse of company documents, and settled the case out of court in 2009.

Huang argued that sharing information publicly benefited the entire company, but executives told the Times they viewed the arrangement as a way for Huang to maintain control and make it harder for anyone to challenge him without being publicly ridiculed.

extraction.body: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.” The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said. He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom. Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources.

passages: Most CEOs worry that their employees aren’t paid enough to stay motivated.
Jensen Huang reportedly had the opposite problem.
The first stakeholder group to watch is Nvidia’s own workforce.
If employees are as financially comfortable as Huang reportedly believed, they are also unusually free to leave.
A culture that leans on embarrassment may work on people who feel they cannot walk away.

The chipmaker’s value rests heavily on its people: the engineers, researchers, and executives who design and ship its products.

passages: “I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston reportedly wrote in notes at the time, describing Nvidia staff being terrorized by Huang at an Nvidia off-site meeting. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston also said that Huang told him at the time that public humiliation was a “rite of passage.”
The New York Times reports that Huang governed Nvidia through humiliation and terror, frequently attacking employees with bizarre and violent verbal attacks.

These personal attacks often took place in front of other coworkers, and were nothing if not creative: Huang reportedly yelled at one executive that he should’ve been aborted, told another employee that he’d rip off their arms and use them to beat that person to death, and told someone else he would scalp them and “pee on your brain.”
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds a near-mythic status in Silicon Valley as the figurehead of the chipmaker powering the AI boom.
Sources at Nvidia, however, told the NYT that they felt their relationship with Huang was akin to Stockholm Syndrome, wherein people become emotionally attached to their abuser.

A spokesperson for Huang responded to Winston’s allegations, calling them “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” but didn’t respond to other questions about Huang’s aggressive behavior, per the report.
I’m a senior staff writer at Futurism, investigating how the rise of artificial intelligence is impacting the media, internet, and information ecosystems.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. extraction.body: Complete protection for your devices, online privacy & identity Combines security, performance & privacy features in one app Enhanced protection with device performance booster Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent? This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.” While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents. Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site. Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites. Here’s how you can protect yourself and your data: We analyze the first-ever real-world incidents where attackers targeted AI agents deployed in corporate environments. extraction.body: Google announced its “agentic era” for Google Gemini back in spring 2025, while Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the other big players in the AI space have each announced their own AI agents. As with any new technology, it’s possible to use these new tools for productivity at work. In fact, that’s why they were designed. The short version is that it’s an AI that can perform actions on behalf of a user. This can be anything from conducting deeper research to literally taking over your mouse and keyboard to perform tasks for you. It’s a very broad and inexact definition, but in short, if it can do more than a chatbot, then it’s largely considered an AI agent. If this is something you want to try, here are the best AI agents you can get right now.Agent.aiTo start the list, there are a number of AI agent services out there that will let you build out your own AI agent for your specific use case. These services include Stack AI, n8n, Gumloop, Agent.ai, and many others. They focus on giving users an easy way to create a custom agent without needing to know how to code. Another similarity that these services have is that they scale out for enterprise use, which is how most of their marketing is done. In any case, of the ones listed above, I think Agent.ai is arguably the best one for beginners. It’s set up like a marketplace of sorts where you can choose AI agents that perform the functions you want. Should one not be available, you can either request that one be made or you can create one yourself. ClaudeAnthropic’s Claude is one of many AI chatbots with an AI agent function that can be taught to do things. This is a solid example of a more hardcore option as you essentially have to build your AI agent yourself using Claude as the AI powering the whole thing. The benefit is that once you get over the learning curve, you can customize your AI agent to do what you want. And why it's becoming my favorite AI tool There are some “agentic tools,” according to Anthropic, that you can access right away. That’s the easiest way to get an AI agent from Anthropic. ChatGPT AgentOpenAI was among the first big AI companies to jump on the AI agent bandwagon over the summer. Its agentic AI is something more in line with what you would expect from an AI agent. You can do things like ask it to check your calendar and brief you on the day ahead or ask it to make you a shopping list. In the future, AI agents will likely be able to complete purchases for you as well, but this functionality is limited.Per OpenAI, ChatGPT performs these tasks on its own “virtual computer” of sorts, where it’ll store your data and recall it as needed, and then create things for you like the aforementioned notes and lists. ChatGPT’s Deep Research function technically falls under this purview as well. The only downside is that you can’t use the feature unless you’re a Pro or Enterprise subscriber. Google GeminiGoogle has dived into the world of AI agents arguably more so than any other company. Gemini CLI is an AI agent that lives in your terminal and helps you do things like fix bugs in your code, create new features, and test your software to make sure it works. This is different from Google’s Gemini Code Assist, which operates like Claude Code in that it creates new code based on natural language prompts. This allows Gemini to see what your browser sees and then tell you about the contents of the webpage. Google has been rapidly improving since it launched, and eventually, Google plans to add functionality that will allow it to actually control the browser on your behalf. So, you would, in theory, be able to tell it to go onto Amazon and order your shampoo, and then it would do it without additional input. To be clear, we're not quite there yet, as Amazon reportedly isn't super excited about AI agents replacing actual customers on its site.Since ChatGPT Deep Research counts as an AI agent, Gemini’s Deep Research feature does as well. That’s accessible from the Gemini chat window. From there, ask it a question and it’ll put together a ton of resources to help research more complex topics. Toss in the ability to build your own AI agent through Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, and that covers almost all of the bases. Microsoft CopilotLike Google, Microsoft has packed AI agents into a lot of its products. That includes Copilot Vision in Edge, which works like Google’s Gemini in Chrome where the AI can interact with your browser and summarize what it sees there.

The only downside is that you can’t use the feature unless you’re a Pro or Enterprise subscriber.
Google GeminiGoogle has dived into the world of AI agents arguably more so than any other company.
Gemini CLI is an AI agent that lives in your terminal and helps you do things like fix bugs in your code, create new features, and test your software to make sure it works.
This is different from Google’s Gemini Code Assist, which operates like Claude Code in that it creates new code based on natural language prompts.
This allows Gemini to see what your browser sees and then tell you about the contents of the webpage.
Google has been rapidly improving since it launched, and eventually, Google plans to add functionality that will allow it to actually control the browser on your behalf.
So, you would, in theory, be able to tell it to go onto Amazon and order your shampoo, and then it would do it without additional input.

To be clear, we're not quite there yet, as Amazon reportedly isn't super excited about AI agents replacing actual customers on its site.Since ChatGPT Deep Research counts as an AI agent, Gemini’s Deep Research feature does as well.
That’s accessible from the Gemini chat window.
From there, ask it a question and it’ll put together a ton of resources to help research more complex topics.
Toss in the ability to build your own AI agent through Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, and that covers almost all of the bases.
Microsoft CopilotLike Google, Microsoft has packed AI agents into a lot of its products.
That includes Copilot Vision in Edge, which works like Google’s Gemini in Chrome where the AI can interact with your browser and summarize what it sees there.

Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent?
It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform.

Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses.
On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent.
As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response.

Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget.
