extraction.body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.” Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”

Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”

How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”

For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

extraction.body: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return. Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.) Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China. What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down. A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027. Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country. It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting. So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way. Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him. It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.” So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen. Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks. Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there. Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that. Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members. passages: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

sources.title: Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels
passages: It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list.
Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list.

Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects.
Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore.

Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground.
And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.
The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country.
Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction.
Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.
Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery.

As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general.
And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. (Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.) As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945. Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel. Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero . Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers. It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play. (WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.) Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.) Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution. Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb. Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film. Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

extraction.body: Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most. (Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.) As I wrote previously , Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One , setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945. Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel. Godzilla Minus On e was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero . Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah , whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers. It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play. (WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.) Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.) Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution. Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield : Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb. Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film. Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

sources.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
passages: Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.
Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act.

extraction.body: Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels. Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

sources.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
passages: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

According to NPR: > Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan. According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: > On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

extraction.body: Inter Miami CF is set to get its Audi 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs campaign underway this Saturday, Nov. 21, hosting Columbus Crew for the first match in the Round One Best-of-3 series between the sides. The first-ever postseason match at Nu Stadium, which is presented by Nu, is slated for 6 a p.m. ET kick off. Show up and support the champions as Inter Miami begins its MLS Cup title defense in the Audi 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs, with Nu providing the entertainment for the evening! Read all about the match presented by Nu HERE . Don’t miss the first-ever Audi MLS Cup Playoffs match at Nu Stadium and get your tickets HERE . Fans are incentivized to take public transportation to Nu Stadium. Fans can now purchase a $10 roundtrip Tri-Rail ticket to the Miami Intermodal Center (MIC) for all remaining Inter Miami CF matches at Nu Stadium in 2026. The ticket includes an exclusive incentive of a $10 food and beverage credit, redeemable by the Guest Services location outside of Section 101 of the stadium. Make sure to check the websites of the respective public transportation services before planning your visits, as schedules and routes might have changed. Secure your single-match parking passes HERE ! PLEASE NOTE: Single-match parking passes are only available on the Yellow Lot , as parking in the Audi Black Lot and the Red Lot is sold out. Fans who plan to park on-site must purchase a parking pass in advance . Due to high demand, parking is expected to sell out, and on-site purchases will not be available on matchday . This policy is in place to ensure a smooth and efficient arrival experience for all guests. Plan your route and arrive early, All information about driving directions and ridesharing options to Nu Stadium is available HERE . To provide a safer environment for the public and to expedite guest entry into the stadium, Nu Stadium policy limits and restricts the size and type of bags that are permitted into the stadium during any events taking place. We encourage guests NOT to bring any bags, however, the following will be permitted after proper screening: Consult Nu Stadium's complete Clear Bag Policy HERE . Fans around the world can tune in to the action live on Apple TV . Inter Miami closed out the 2026 regular season with a 3-3 draw at home against Charlotte FC on MLS Decision Day. Goals from defender Ian Fray, midfielder Rodrigo De Paul, and Luis Suárez secured the point at Nu Stadium. Inter Miami recorded 16 wins, six losses, and 12 draws this MLS regular season for a total 60 points and finished second in the Eastern Conference standings. Notably, Inter Miami was the top goal-scoring team in MLS this regular season with 80 total goals in 34 games, six more than the next highest-scoring side. Messi, the reigning MLS Landon Donovan MVP Award winner, led the league in goals with 26 strikes in 31 appearances and made history by becoming the first player to win the MLS Golden Boot presented by Audi in consecutive season. Messi also led the squad in asissts throughout the regular season with 17, followed by De Paul with 16 and Telasco Segovia with 13. Following Saturday's match, Game 2 will see Inter Miami play on the road against Columbus at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field in Columbus, Ohio on Friday, Nov. 27 at 8 p.m. ET. If needed, the series will return to Miami for Game 3 on Tuesday, Dec. 1 or Wednesday, Dec. 2, with the kick off time TBD. This will be Inter Miami's fifth appearance in Audi MLS Cup Playoffs, with Club looking to defend its title after capping off a stellar postseason run in 2025 by clinching the title with a 3-1 victory over the Vancouver Whitecaps in the 2025 MLS Cup. Prior to winning the championship, Inter Miami had featured in the postseason in 2020 (Play-In Round), 2022 (Round One), and 2024 (Round One). Saturday's meeting presents the 14th matchup between the sides in Club history. Inter Miami leads the series with seven wins to four for Columbus Crew, while two other matchups restulted in a draw. The two 2026 MLS regular season games between the sides presented a 2-2 draw at home in August and a 2-1 loss on the road in September for Inter Miami. Columbus Crew secured a playoffs berth with a seventh-place finish in the Eastern Conference, putting together a record of 14 wins, 15 losses, and five draws for a total 47 points. Spanish midfielder Brais Méndez was the Crew's main threat in attack throughout the regular season, contributing six goals and four assists in 14 appearances.

extraction.body: Inter Miami begin their MLS Cup title defence on Saturday when they host the Columbus Crew at Nu Stadium in game one of that best-of-three series. The defending champions finished second in the Eastern Conference by two points, drawing their final regular-season outing at home to Charlotte FC, 3-3, while the Crew snuck in as the seventh seed with a thrilling 4-3 win over the Chicago Fire. Miami will hope to take the first step toward more history on Saturday as they aim to become the first Eastern Conference club this century to capture consecutive MLS Cups. If they can pull it off, they would be the first MLS side to do so since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2011 and 2012 and the second ever to achieve that feat in the East, after DC United.. Kily Gonzalez has seen his team drop points in three of their last four league encounters, though they have only suffered one defeat since October. Thanks in large part to captain Lionel Messi , Miami led the regular season in goals with 80, one fewer than they managed a year ago. The Herons also led the league in goals per match (2.4) and have netted three or more times in four of their last five post-season outings. Saturday will mark the first time they meet Columbus in the playoffs, and Inter Miami having never lost a home game against the Crew. A team that could barely buy a win at the start of the regular season could seemingly do no wrong down the stretch of it. The Crew began 2026 without a win in their first five league games but will enter the playoffs as one of the hottest teams remaining, riding a six-match winning streak. Laurent Courtois has unlocked this team’s scoring potential, with Columbus netting multiple times in nine straight MLS affairs, with three or more goals in four of those instances. This weekend they can end a three-match playoff losing run away from home, having won just one post-season affair since lifting the MLS Cup in 2023. As potent as they have been in front of goal lately, this side have rarely shown much defensive poise away from home, conceding three or more goals in seven MLS games this year outside of ScottsMiracle-Gro Field. Columbus won their only previous playoff game in the Sunshine State, defeating Orlando City 2-0 in 2023 en route to winning the MLS Cup later that year. A shoulder issue will likely keep Mateo Silvetti on the Miami sidelines on Saturday, while Tadeo Allende is dealing with a knee problem, Israel Boatwright is recovering from a cruciate ligament tear and Cesar Abadia is doubtful due to a groin strain. Messi finished the regular season as the top goalscorer for a second year running, though it was Ian Fray, Luis Suarez and Rodrigo De Paul who netted for them on Decision Day. There is one injury concern on the Columbus side heading into this encounter as Wessam Abou Ali is doubtful because of a knee injury. Gonzalo Tapia notched a brace for the Crew against the Fire, with Anass Zaroury and Brais Mendez also scoring, with the latter netting the winner in stoppage time. We often see these teams throw caution to the wind and play in an all-out attack mode, and if that happens, as we anticipate in game one, the home team is more likely to come out on top given their firepower. extraction.body: Inter Miami CF is set to get its Audi 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs campaign underway this Saturday, Nov. 21, hosting Columbus Crew for the first match in the Round One Best-of-3 series between the sides. The first-ever postseason match at Nu Stadium, which is presented by Nu, is slated for 6 a p.m. ET kick off. Show up and support the champions as Inter Miami begins its MLS Cup title defense in the Audi 2026 MLS Cup Playoffs, with Nu providing the entertainment for the evening! Read all about the match presented by Nu HERE . Don’t miss the first-ever Audi MLS Cup Playoffs match at Nu Stadium and get your tickets HERE . Fans are incentivized to take public transportation to Nu Stadium. Fans can now purchase a $10 roundtrip Tri-Rail ticket to the Miami Intermodal Center (MIC) for all remaining Inter Miami CF matches at Nu Stadium in 2026. The ticket includes an exclusive incentive of a $10 food and beverage credit, redeemable by the Guest Services location outside of Section 101 of the stadium. Make sure to check the websites of the respective public transportation services before planning your visits, as schedules and routes might have changed. Secure your single-match parking passes HERE ! PLEASE NOTE: Single-match parking passes are only available on the Yellow Lot , as parking in the Audi Black Lot and the Red Lot is sold out. Fans who plan to park on-site must purchase a parking pass in advance . Due to high demand, parking is expected to sell out, and on-site purchases will not be available on matchday . This policy is in place to ensure a smooth and efficient arrival experience for all guests. Plan your route and arrive early, All information about driving directions and ridesharing options to Nu Stadium is available HERE . To provide a safer environment for the public and to expedite guest entry into the stadium, Nu Stadium policy limits and restricts the size and type of bags that are permitted into the stadium during any events taking place. We encourage guests NOT to bring any bags, however, the following will be permitted after proper screening: Consult Nu Stadium's complete Clear Bag Policy HERE . Fans around the world can tune in to the action live on Apple TV . Inter Miami closed out the 2026 regular season with a 3-3 draw at home against Charlotte FC on MLS Decision Day. Goals from defender Ian Fray, midfielder Rodrigo De Paul, and Luis Suárez secured the point at Nu Stadium. Inter Miami recorded 16 wins, six losses, and 12 draws this MLS regular season for a total 60 points and finished second in the Eastern Conference standings. Notably, Inter Miami was the top goal-scoring team in MLS this regular season with 80 total goals in 34 games, six more than the next highest-scoring side. Messi, the reigning MLS Landon Donovan MVP Award winner, led the league in goals with 26 strikes in 31 appearances and made history by becoming the first player to win the MLS Golden Boot presented by Audi in consecutive season. Messi also led the squad in asissts throughout the regular season with 17, followed by De Paul with 16 and Telasco Segovia with 13. Following Saturday's match, Game 2 will see Inter Miami play on the road against Columbus at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field in Columbus, Ohio on Friday, Nov. 27 at 8 p.m. ET. If needed, the series will return to Miami for Game 3 on Tuesday, Dec. 1 or Wednesday, Dec. 2, with the kick off time TBD. This will be Inter Miami's fifth appearance in Audi MLS Cup Playoffs, with Club looking to defend its title after capping off a stellar postseason run in 2025 by clinching the title with a 3-1 victory over the Vancouver Whitecaps in the 2025 MLS Cup. Prior to winning the championship, Inter Miami had featured in the postseason in 2020 (Play-In Round), 2022 (Round One), and 2024 (Round One). Saturday's meeting presents the 14th matchup between the sides in Club history. Inter Miami leads the series with seven wins to four for Columbus Crew, while two other matchups restulted in a draw. The two 2026 MLS regular season games between the sides presented a 2-2 draw at home in August and a 2-1 loss on the road in September for Inter Miami. Columbus Crew secured a playoffs berth with a seventh-place finish in the Eastern Conference, putting together a record of 14 wins, 15 losses, and five draws for a total 47 points. Spanish midfielder Brais Méndez was the Crew's main threat in attack throughout the regular season, contributing six goals and four assists in 14 appearances.

extraction.body: Inter Miami begin their MLS Cup title defence on Saturday when they host the Columbus Crew at Nu Stadium in game one of that best-of-three series. The defending champions finished second in the Eastern Conference by two points, drawing their final regular-season outing at home to Charlotte FC, 3-3, while the Crew snuck in as the seventh seed with a thrilling 4-3 win over the Chicago Fire. Miami will hope to take the first step toward more history on Saturday as they aim to become the first Eastern Conference club this century to capture consecutive MLS Cups. If they can pull it off, they would be the first MLS side to do so since the Los Angeles Galaxy in 2011 and 2012 and the second ever to achieve that feat in the East, after DC United.. Kily Gonzalez has seen his team drop points in three of their last four league encounters, though they have only suffered one defeat since October. Thanks in large part to captain Lionel Messi , Miami led the regular season in goals with 80, one fewer than they managed a year ago. The Herons also led the league in goals per match (2.4) and have netted three or more times in four of their last five post-season outings. Saturday will mark the first time they meet Columbus in the playoffs, and Inter Miami having never lost a home game against the Crew. A team that could barely buy a win at the start of the regular season could seemingly do no wrong down the stretch of it. The Crew began 2026 without a win in their first five league games but will enter the playoffs as one of the hottest teams remaining, riding a six-match winning streak. Laurent Courtois has unlocked this team’s scoring potential, with Columbus netting multiple times in nine straight MLS affairs, with three or more goals in four of those instances. This weekend they can end a three-match playoff losing run away from home, having won just one post-season affair since lifting the MLS Cup in 2023. As potent as they have been in front of goal lately, this side have rarely shown much defensive poise away from home, conceding three or more goals in seven MLS games this year outside of ScottsMiracle-Gro Field. Columbus won their only previous playoff game in the Sunshine State, defeating Orlando City 2-0 in 2023 en route to winning the MLS Cup later that year. A shoulder issue will likely keep Mateo Silvetti on the Miami sidelines on Saturday, while Tadeo Allende is dealing with a knee problem, Israel Boatwright is recovering from a cruciate ligament tear and Cesar Abadia is doubtful due to a groin strain. Messi finished the regular season as the top goalscorer for a second year running, though it was Ian Fray, Luis Suarez and Rodrigo De Paul who netted for them on Decision Day. There is one injury concern on the Columbus side heading into this encounter as Wessam Abou Ali is doubtful because of a knee injury. Gonzalo Tapia notched a brace for the Crew against the Fire, with Anass Zaroury and Brais Mendez also scoring, with the latter netting the winner in stoppage time. We often see these teams throw caution to the wind and play in an all-out attack mode, and if that happens, as we anticipate in game one, the home team is more likely to come out on top given their firepower. In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge wrote in a paper this week, "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis." As you're no doubt already aware, and as Alpöge explains, the Riemann Hypothesis is the classic problem in number theory and one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics. Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined. "The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all interesting solutions of the equation ζ(s) = 0 lie on a certain vertical straight line," the Clay Mathematics Institute explains. "This has been checked for the first 10,000,000,000,000 solutions. A proof that it is true for every interesting solution would shed light on many of the mysteries surrounding the distribution of prime numbers." As Scientific American notes , the problem is the "North Star for the entire field of number theory, and the most famous open problem in math." Furthermore, the problem was previously thought so insurmountable that experts didn't even bother working on it. Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes. This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy . Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." "In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds. Alpöge not only believes that he has used Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, but also believes the method could easily extend to the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and the Extended Riemann Hypothesis, too. "An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.

This would not be the first time that AI has made a significant discovery or finding in a major STEM field. Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy .

Alpöge's statement is not without reservation. Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."
"In a time of revolution in mathematics, I hope the argument provides a glimpse towards the miracles that lie ahead," Alpöge adds.

extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. extraction.body: Home » General » Business » Mathematicians claim proof of 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis using AI, human methods New Delhi, Nov 21 (SocialNews.XYZ) Two mathematicians have made competing claims to have solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems, setting up a rare contest between an AI-assisted approach and a proof developed through human mathematical reasoning. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic, earlier this week said that he had discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis with assistance from Anthropic's Claude AI model. Alessandro Maria Masullo, a researcher at Stanford University, on the same day forwarded a separate proof of the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which Stanford mathematician Ravi Vakil described as having been developed without AI assistance. While Alpöge's work has cleared several important computer-based verification checks, Masullo’s proof has attracted queries from mathematicians examining the draft. However, the problems reported by several mathematicians were also identified with them using assistance from different AI models. Vakil said the issues would need to be resolved before Masullo’s proof could be accepted. Alpöge released a four-page note and a 14-part archive containing nearly 17.4 million lines of Lean code, a mathematical language used to formalise and verify proofs. He said the work also establishes the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions. The Riemann hypothesis was proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, as a mathematical theory on the pattern in which prime numbers appear. Prime numbers, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11, are divisible only by themselves and 1. Riemann's hypothesis attempts to explain the pattern in which these numbers appear, through a mathematical function, namely, Riemann zeta function. Proving the hypothesis is among seven major mathematical challenges identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. However, a proposed proof must undergo at least two years of scrutiny after appearing in a qualifying peer-reviewed journal. extraction.body: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics. “The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems. The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory. Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this … But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯. It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully. Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding. Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue. Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer. Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.” Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it. In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.” This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources. Examples include 2, 3 and 5.Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, the Riemann hypothesis predicts that their distribution follows a deeper mathematical pattern. Each carries a prize of $1 million for a correct solution.Alpöge's announcement follows a series of AI-assisted advances in mathematics, with large language models increasingly being used to explore complex conjectures and theoretical problems. The latest claim, if verified, would represent a major step beyond earlier results that established the predicted pattern for only a proportion of certain mathematical values.Why the proposed proof mattersYouness Lamzouri, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France, said the proposed result would go substantially further than an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough.Previous work had established that at least 67.25% of a particular set of mathematical values followed the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. coreStoryFacts.text: In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis.
"An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.
Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined.
Alpöge's statement is not without reservation.
Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding.

"It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

Earlier this year, OpenAI helped create a breakthrough solution for the Navier-Stokes problem, a finding somewhat overshadowed by a plagiarism controversy .
Anthropic has been busy celebrating the incredible numbers from its record-breaking $1.7tn stock market debut on Thursday.
But one of its mathematicians has been setting records of a very different kind — they claim to have used Claude AI to prove a 167-year-old mathematics theory that's stumped professors for decades.
One thing's for sure — 2027 is going to be a very interesting year indeed for math and the sciences.
This is likely the start of a new math journey, where the proof will need to be vetted independently by other mathematicians and experts in the field.
It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis).
However, the competition's rules state that proofs need "two years of scrutiny" before a potential payout.
The discovery is a sign of what can be achieved when the world's best researchers are given access to the world's best frontier models.
This theory is based on the conundrum of prime numbers and proposes that there might be a hidden pattern behind them.
In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.
No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says.
Referring to Anthropic's recent IPO, Alpöge also says the "timing is horrible" — because it could lead some to conclude that the findings are somewhat contrived.
"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added.

The proposed proof also addresses the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader version of the original conjecture.The claim has drawn attention from leading mathematicians, although the proof still needs wider independent scrutiny and a deeper understanding of its mathematical reasoning. James Maynard, the Regius Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford and a 2022 Fields Medal winner, expressed optimism about the result.“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics, establishing one of the great mysteries of the subject,” Maynard told IBM Think in an interview. “This result really stands out, even in the context of all the recent AI breakthroughs.”Alpöge shared the proposed proof in Lean, a programming language and proof assistant that checks mathematical arguments step by step. The format allows researchers to examine whether each part of the reasoning follows logically, although verifying the computer-checked argument and understanding the ideas behind it are separate challenges.In a statement posted on his website, Alpöge wrote: “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.”What is the Riemann hypothesis?First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, which are divisible only by themselves and one. Examples include 2, 3 and 5.Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, the Riemann hypothesis predicts that their distribution follows a deeper mathematical pattern. Each carries a prize of $1 million for a correct solution.Alpöge's announcement follows a series of AI-assisted advances in mathematics, with large language models increasingly being used to explore complex conjectures and theoretical problems. The latest claim, if verified, would represent a major step beyond earlier results that established the predicted pattern for only a proportion of certain mathematical values.Why the proposed proof mattersYouness Lamzouri, a professor of mathematics at the University of Lorraine in France, said the proposed result would go substantially further than an earlier AI-assisted breakthrough.Previous work had established that at least 67.25% of a particular set of mathematical values followed the pattern predicted by the Riemann hypothesis. The new claim, if correct, would establish that all of them follow the pattern without exception.Lamzouri, who developed a shorter proof of the earlier result without AI, said the latest announcement had left him astonished.“I don’t have words to describe what I am feeling right now. “If this claim happens to be true, it will be a huge achievement.”However, he cautioned that checking the computer-generated proof would only be the first step. Mathematicians would also need to understand the reasoning and ideas behind it before accepting its broader implications.“Mathematics is mainly about understanding why something is true,” he said. I know there will be a wide range of reactions in our community, but to me this is a human triumph, and a day for celebration.”Sutherland said the achievement should also be viewed in the context of the human work behind the development of Lean, large language models and centuries of mathematical research.“There is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof,” he said. But perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.”A turning point for AI-assisted mathematics?Alpöge's claim comes after a year of growing attention on the ability of AI models to tackle difficult mathematical problems. He had earlier attracted attention in July after sharing a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture. He was also involved in a September controversy surrounding an OpenAI mathematical result related to the Navier-Stokes problem.If the Riemann hypothesis proof is independently verified and its reasoning understood, it could mark a major advance in the use of AI for mathematical discovery. The result would not necessarily have immediate practical applications, but it could reshape research in number theory and deepen understanding of connections across mathematics.For now, the central question is whether the proposed proof withstands independent examination. Even if the computer verification holds, mathematicians will need to establish why the argument works and what new avenues it opens.You use AI every day.
