extraction.body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, has claimed to have proved the Riemann hypothesis with the help of a large language model. In a statement on his website, he said he believed he had discovered the proof while working with Claude. The announcement came on a Friday, a day after Anthropic's record-breaking debut on the stock market. The Riemann hypothesis was proposed in 1859 by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It concerns the distribution of prime numbers along the number line. It has long been the guiding problem of number theory. The Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize for its solution, and progress was so rare that many leading experts devoted little time to it, since no clear route to a proof existed. Alpöge says his proof establishes the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a far broader version of the original conjecture. Many results across mathematics are currently conditional on it, so a proof would immediately turn them into established truths. Errors can still arise in how a statement is encoded in Lean, so experts must confirm that the hypothesis has been formalised correctly and that the proof is sound. Andrew Sutherland of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology said he independently compiled the result in Lean. The publication reporting the claim has also carried a follow-up saying independent mathematicians consider the proof almost certainly true, though that report is not reproduced here. Hector Pasten of the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile said a correct and well-understood proof would complete a dictionary between branches of mathematics whose connections were previously partial, something like a Rosetta Stone. Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that even a first reading suggested the proof's new ideas could open fresh avenues in number theory. Its importance lies in what it would demonstrate about the intellectual reach of machines. In July, he posted a Claude-generated solution to the Jacobian conjecture, which began an unusually eventful summer for the discipline. He was also central to a September controversy involving OpenAI and the Navier-Stokes problem, in which New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster implied that the company had used his and Alpöge's work improperly. An earlier breakthrough came in October, when one of the results in a large release of mathematics from OpenAI made notable progress in understanding the primes. The claim follows a year in which AI systems moved from unreliable problem-solvers to tools of exceptional power across the discipline. Alpöge's statement acknowledges the sense of loss many mathematicians feel, yet he describes what he witnessed as the dawn of something far greater across science. Sutherland offered a similar perspective, suggesting the most important step in the proof was the building of a machine capable of thinking. He also credited the human effort behind Lean, language models and the centuries of mathematics on which they rest.

facts.text: In the same week that Anthropic was floated on the Nasdaq in its initial public offering , a mathematician employed by the company claims to have discovered proof behind one of the world's most famous math problem, the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis.
"An astounding amount of mathematics is present in the argument, far more than I had imagined would be necessary as a student," he writes.
Proposed in 1859 by Bernhard Riemann, who gave the problem its name, it is the theory that prime numbers are not in fact random but determined.
Alpöge's statement is not without reservation.
Aside from confirming whether Claude has actually helped crack the Riemann Hypothesis, which will take some time, he admits sadness at the finding.

"It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

One thing's for sure — 2027 is going to be a very interesting year indeed for math and the sciences.
This is likely the start of a new math journey, where the proof will need to be vetted independently by other mathematicians and experts in the field.
It'll also be a contender for the Millennium Prize, which offers a $1 million prize for solving seven major math problems (including the Riemann Hypothesis).
However, the competition's rules state that proofs need "two years of scrutiny" before a potential payout.
The discovery is a sign of what can be achieved when the world's best researchers are given access to the world's best frontier models.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.
No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line," he says.

"This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood, and I am very touchy about the treatment of great intellectual goals," he added.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump on Saturday seemed to downplay a breach into the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, using the incident to revisit his longstanding and unrelated grievances with the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News when asked about the breach. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.” The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers, which was first reported by CNN, is the second such breach in recent months, coming as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system. But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach. The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. extraction.body: President Donald Trump on Saturday seemed to downplay a breach into the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, using the incident to revisit his longstanding and unrelated grievances with the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. “I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News when asked about the breach. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.” The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers, which was first reported by CNN, is the second such breach in recent months, coming as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system. But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach. The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. “Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants, and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety. My concern isn’t simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website. A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported. In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported. During his Fox News interview, Trump implied that the latest breach could uncover information about his 2019 phone call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the president was accused of pressuring Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden, leading to his first impeachment by the House of Representatives. “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” Trump said, without citing evidence, as he listed “other hoaxes” he said the breach could reveal information about. “I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany. “So as soon as you said that, and as soon as I heard about it a little bit before, I said, ‘Well, that’s an interesting situation. I wonder who’s doing it because wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?’” Trump during his first term repeatedly criticized the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and potential links to his campaign. At one point before the election that year, he encouraged Russian officials accused of hacking into the Democratic National Committee’s computer system to publish any incriminating emails related to his opponent, former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, which they then tried to do, according to a 2018 federal indictment filed against 12 Russian intelligence operatives. The president on Saturday declined to share specific information on the intrusion into the FBI’s system, which serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement.

facts.text: President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”
In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack .

“But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.” The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers, which was first reported by CNN, is the second such breach in recent months, coming as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system.

President Donald Trump on Saturday seemed to downplay a breach into the FBI’s nationwide criminal information database, using the incident to revisit his longstanding and unrelated grievances with the FBI over its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election.
“I will say that it’s not good — I don’t like that,” Trump said during a telephone interview with Fox News when asked about the breach.

During his Fox News interview, Trump implied that the latest breach could uncover information about his 2019 phone call Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, during which the president was accused of pressuring Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden, leading to his first impeachment by the House of Representatives.

“We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” The NCIC database is one of the most critical information-sharing systems in law enforcement, a former FBI official who led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN.
“I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump told the interviewer, his former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany.
But two people briefed on the issue said the agency is investigating the breach.
“We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good,” Trump said.

However, Trump suggested the breach might expose previously undisclosed information concerning investigations involving Russia, Ukraine and alleged election fraud.

passages: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years.

extraction.body: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.” The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said. He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom. Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources.

passages: The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources.
Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people.
Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits.
Huang reportedly defended the public humiliation as a “rite of passage,” saying he subjected new employees to it during their first six months to see whether they could tolerate it.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.
Despite the accounts of his behavior, Huang also inspired considerable loyalty among Nvidia employees, some of whom have publicly called for his return since his departure.
Thousands reportedly signed a letter asking him to come back, while others have defended his leadership, crediting his technical expertise, vision, and personal support, according to the Times.
Some employees even have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo.
Huang’s treatment of employees reportedly continued as Nvidia grew into a $5 trillion company, per the Times.
In one instance, he publicly mocked an executive who took his children camping, suggesting he needed to find someone more committed to the job.
He also repeatedly made fun of another executive’s interest in aviation.
In 2007, former Nvidia attorney Stephen Pettigrew sued the company, alleging age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s complaints.
He said the company's conduct had caused him to seek emergency medical attention for severe anxiety and nervous tension.
Nvidia denied wrongdoing, countersued over alleged contract violations and misuse of company documents, and settled the case out of court in 2009.

Huang argued that sharing information publicly benefited the entire company, but executives told the Times they viewed the arrangement as a way for Huang to maintain control and make it harder for anyone to challenge him without being publicly ridiculed.

passages: “I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Winston reportedly wrote in notes at the time, describing Nvidia staff being terrorized by Huang at an Nvidia off-site meeting. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.” Winston also said that Huang told him at the time that public humiliation was a “rite of passage.”
The New York Times reports that Huang governed Nvidia through humiliation and terror, frequently attacking employees with bizarre and violent verbal attacks.

These personal attacks often took place in front of other coworkers, and were nothing if not creative: Huang reportedly yelled at one executive that he should’ve been aborted, told another employee that he’d rip off their arms and use them to beat that person to death, and told someone else he would scalp them and “pee on your brain.”
Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds a near-mythic status in Silicon Valley as the figurehead of the chipmaker powering the AI boom.
Sources at Nvidia, however, told the NYT that they felt their relationship with Huang was akin to Stockholm Syndrome, wherein people become emotionally attached to their abuser.

A spokesperson for Huang responded to Winston’s allegations, calling them “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” but didn’t respond to other questions about Huang’s aggressive behavior, per the report.

extraction.body: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff. He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation. This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.” The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said. He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability. Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times. Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993. Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom. Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave. But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards. In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources.

Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show.
He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness.
He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them.

And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.” The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution.
They were also foundational to Huang’s management style. “I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years.
The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.
Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees.
Both those who liked Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish.
Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world.

In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career.
Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset.
But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.) Huang denied Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired.
They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said.
Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Huang’s behavior.
Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Huang or forge a new way forward.
She will do so in the face of pressure from Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company.
Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles.
Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards.
Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.
He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business.

He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.
Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Huang for more than a decade.
Some shared Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees.
If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
But in the eyes of some, Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.
In September 2004, Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources.

passages: The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources.
Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people.
Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.
Despite the accounts of his behavior, Huang also inspired considerable loyalty among Nvidia employees, some of whom have publicly called for his return since his departure.
Thousands reportedly signed a letter asking him to come back, while others have defended his leadership, crediting his technical expertise, vision, and personal support, according to the Times.
Some employees even have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo.

In one instance, he publicly mocked an executive who took his children camping, suggesting he needed to find someone more committed to the job.

In 2007, former Nvidia attorney Stephen Pettigrew sued the company, alleging age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s complaints.
He said the company's conduct had caused him to seek emergency medical attention for severe anxiety and nervous tension.
Nvidia denied wrongdoing, countersued over alleged contract violations and misuse of company documents, and settled the case out of court in 2009.

Huang argued that sharing information publicly benefited the entire company, but executives told the Times they viewed the arrangement as a way for Huang to maintain control and make it harder for anyone to challenge him without being publicly ridiculed.

The chipmaker’s value rests heavily on its people: the engineers, researchers, and executives who design and ship its products.

extraction.body: Can’t-miss innovations from the bleeding edge of science and tech Disgraced Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang holds a near-mythic status in Silicon Valley as the figurehead of the chipmaker powering the AI boom. He also, according to new reporting, could be an absolute nightmare as a boss. The New York Times reports that Huang governed Nvidia through humiliation and terror, frequently attacking employees with bizarre and violent verbal attacks. These personal attacks often took place in front of other coworkers, and were nothing if not creative: Huang reportedly yelled at one executive that he should’ve been aborted, told another employee that he’d rip off their arms and use them to beat that person to death, and told someone else he would scalp them and “pee on your brain.” Some Nvidia insiders told the NYT that Huang once walked around a room of employees telling them he’d kill them, before stopping in front of an older employee, who was in their 70s, to declare that everyone hoped he’d just die. The reporting sheds new light on Huang’s stewardship of Nvidia, now the biggest company in the world, as the embattled founder — and the world — grapple with his shocking ouster amid revelations of sex scandal and espionage. Huang resigned from his role at Nvidia this month after it was revealed that he’d had extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and multiple Nvidia staffers, including a direct report . Seen by many in the tech world as a hero of the AI boom, Huang has received an outpouring of support from across the tech industry — and even from the president of the United States, with whom Huang is close. Thousands of Nvidia staff have signed a petition urging for his reinstatement, as have many tech and business leaders . Sources at Nvidia, however, told the NYT that they felt their relationship with Huang was akin to Stockholm Syndrome, wherein people become emotionally attached to their abuser. Huang also had a practice of speaking to groups of employees at a time as opposed to holding one-on-ones, which the now-former CEO billed as a way to create transparency — yet others saw as a power play that allowed Huang to berate managers in front of their staff, while also putting employees in a position where, should they want to confront their CEO, they’d have to do with others present. Some Nvidia insiders told the NYT that Huang once walked around a room of employees telling them he’d kill them, before stopping in front of an older employee, who was in their 70s, to declare that everyone hoped he’d just die.

Huang resigned from his role at Nvidia this month after it was revealed that he’d had extramarital affairs with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and multiple Nvidia staffers, including a direct report . story.title: How Jensen Huang Made Humiliation Routine at Nvidia - The New York Times

facts.text: By Emily Steel, Kalley Huang, Ryan Mac and Tripp Mickle As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years.

In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Huang. ‘It Pained Me’ Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles.
They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Fisher said.
The behavior reportedly dates back at least to 2004, when Michael Winston joined Nvidia as senior vice president of human resources.
Within weeks, he witnessed Huang verbally attacking employees during a two-day company retreat attended by about 50 people.
Winston later confronted Huang, warning that the conduct could expose Nvidia to lawsuits.
Huang reportedly defended the public humiliation as a “rite of passage,” saying he subjected new employees to it during their first six months to see whether they could tolerate it.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang reportedly spent decades publicly humiliating employees, making violent threats, and ridiculing people in front of their colleagues, sometimes calling the treatment a necessary part of working at the company.
Despite the accounts of his behavior, Huang also inspired considerable loyalty among Nvidia employees, some of whom have publicly called for his return since his departure.
Thousands reportedly signed a letter asking him to come back, while others have defended his leadership, crediting his technical expertise, vision, and personal support, according to the Times.
Some employees even have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo.
Huang’s treatment of employees reportedly continued as Nvidia grew into a $5 trillion company, per the Times.
In one instance, he publicly mocked an executive who took his children camping, suggesting he needed to find someone more committed to the job.
He also repeatedly made fun of another executive’s interest in aviation.
In 2007, former Nvidia attorney Stephen Pettigrew sued the company, alleging age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Winston’s complaints.
He said the company's conduct had caused him to seek emergency medical attention for severe anxiety and nervous tension.
Nvidia denied wrongdoing, countersued over alleged contract violations and misuse of company documents, and settled the case out of court in 2009.

Huang argued that sharing information publicly benefited the entire company, but executives told the Times they viewed the arrangement as a way for Huang to maintain control and make it harder for anyone to challenge him without being publicly ridiculed.

Jensen Huang reportedly had the opposite problem.
The first stakeholder group to watch is Nvidia’s own workforce.
If employees are as financially comfortable as Huang reportedly believed, they are also unusually free to leave.
A culture that leans on embarrassment may work on people who feel they cannot walk away.

Wealthy people respond less to financial carrots.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future. The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

extraction.body: Complete protection for your devices, online privacy & identity Combines security, performance & privacy features in one app Enhanced protection with device performance booster Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent? This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.” While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents. Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site. Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites. extraction.body: Google announced its “agentic era” for Google Gemini back in spring 2025, while Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the other big players in the AI space have each announced their own AI agents. As with any new technology, it’s possible to use these new tools for productivity at work. In fact, that’s why they were designed. The short version is that it’s an AI that can perform actions on behalf of a user. This can be anything from conducting deeper research to literally taking over your mouse and keyboard to perform tasks for you. It’s a very broad and inexact definition, but in short, if it can do more than a chatbot, then it’s largely considered an AI agent. If this is something you want to try, here are the best AI agents you can get right now.Agent.aiTo start the list, there are a number of AI agent services out there that will let you build out your own AI agent for your specific use case. These services include Stack AI, n8n, Gumloop, Agent.ai, and many others. They focus on giving users an easy way to create a custom agent without needing to know how to code. Another similarity that these services have is that they scale out for enterprise use, which is how most of their marketing is done. In any case, of the ones listed above, I think Agent.ai is arguably the best one for beginners. It’s set up like a marketplace of sorts where you can choose AI agents that perform the functions you want. Should one not be available, you can either request that one be made or you can create one yourself. ClaudeAnthropic’s Claude is one of many AI chatbots with an AI agent function that can be taught to do things. This is a solid example of a more hardcore option as you essentially have to build your AI agent yourself using Claude as the AI powering the whole thing. The benefit is that once you get over the learning curve, you can customize your AI agent to do what you want. And why it's becoming my favorite AI tool There are some “agentic tools,” according to Anthropic, that you can access right away. That’s the easiest way to get an AI agent from Anthropic. ChatGPT AgentOpenAI was among the first big AI companies to jump on the AI agent bandwagon over the summer. Its agentic AI is something more in line with what you would expect from an AI agent. You can do things like ask it to check your calendar and brief you on the day ahead or ask it to make you a shopping list. In the future, AI agents will likely be able to complete purchases for you as well, but this functionality is limited.Per OpenAI, ChatGPT performs these tasks on its own “virtual computer” of sorts, where it’ll store your data and recall it as needed, and then create things for you like the aforementioned notes and lists. ChatGPT’s Deep Research function technically falls under this purview as well. The only downside is that you can’t use the feature unless you’re a Pro or Enterprise subscriber. Google GeminiGoogle has dived into the world of AI agents arguably more so than any other company. Gemini CLI is an AI agent that lives in your terminal and helps you do things like fix bugs in your code, create new features, and test your software to make sure it works. This is different from Google’s Gemini Code Assist, which operates like Claude Code in that it creates new code based on natural language prompts. This allows Gemini to see what your browser sees and then tell you about the contents of the webpage. Google has been rapidly improving since it launched, and eventually, Google plans to add functionality that will allow it to actually control the browser on your behalf. So, you would, in theory, be able to tell it to go onto Amazon and order your shampoo, and then it would do it without additional input. To be clear, we're not quite there yet, as Amazon reportedly isn't super excited about AI agents replacing actual customers on its site.Since ChatGPT Deep Research counts as an AI agent, Gemini’s Deep Research feature does as well. That’s accessible from the Gemini chat window. From there, ask it a question and it’ll put together a ton of resources to help research more complex topics. Toss in the ability to build your own AI agent through Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, and that covers almost all of the bases. Microsoft CopilotLike Google, Microsoft has packed AI agents into a lot of its products. That includes Copilot Vision in Edge, which works like Google’s Gemini in Chrome where the AI can interact with your browser and summarize what it sees there.

As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future. The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.” While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents. Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site. Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites. story.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages

facts.text: The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages.
Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform.
Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent?
It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform.

Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses.
On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent.
As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response.
Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device.
Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget.

sources.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
passages: Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said.
“All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”

Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default.
Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

passages: Signal president Meredith Whittaker framed it starkly, calling the OS-level AI integrations "an existential threat" to the app's mission and arguing that Apple, Google and Microsoft are reshaping the environment every app runs in "in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy."

The move extends a tactic Signal first used last year against Microsoft's Recall, the Windows feature that captured periodic screenshots; the company blocked it to keep Recall from storing images of Signal messages by default.

Signal also conceded the fix is incomplete: It doesn't stop sneakier methods of access, such as pulling data straight from a device's filesystem, and it can't yet be implemented on macOS, where Signal says Apple lacks the documented tools to block screenshots reliably.

The privacy-focused company also called on the three OS giants to give developers a simple, well-documented way to opt apps out of AI data access, and to publish clear specifications on how their agents actually handle data, saying it has spent months on "forensic investigations" just to understand what these systems do. Meta's Muse AI Agent Read a User's Private iMessages. Then It Lied About How Signal also flagged third-party agents like Meta's Muse, warning they exploit accessibility permissions meant to help people, not to serve as "a skeleton key" for AI. Signal's move lands amid a broader reckoning over AI agents accessing data they shouldn't, from rogue agents breaching systems to banks scrambling to keep autonomous software out of sensitive accounts.

Once that happens, the content lands in whatever local database or remote server the AI is using, outside Signal's control and beyond the encryption guarantees that have defined the app for a decade.

Signal president Meredith Whittaker framed it starkly, calling the OS-level AI integrations "an existential threat" to the app's mission and arguing that Apple, Google and Microsoft are reshaping the environment every app runs in "in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy."

Users who still want to take screenshots can disable the protection in Signal's settings, though the company warns that doing so could expose their messages, and their contacts' messages, to the AI agents.

Signal also conceded the fix is incomplete: It doesn't stop sneakier methods of access, such as pulling data straight from a device's filesystem, and it can't yet be implemented on macOS, where Signal says Apple lacks the documented tools to block screenshots reliably.

The privacy-focused company also called on the three OS giants to give developers a simple, well-documented way to opt apps out of AI data access, and to publish clear specifications on how their agents actually handle data, saying it has spent months on "forensic investigations" just to understand what these systems do.

Signal also flagged third-party agents like Meta's Muse, warning they exploit accessibility permissions meant to help people, not to serve as "a skeleton key" for AI.

The worry isn't hypothetical: A journalist found that Muse had accessed his private iMessages despite his settings and then gave a false explanation of how it knew their contents, an episode that crystallized fears about how much agents can reach once granted deep device permissions.

Signal's move lands amid a broader reckoning over AI agents accessing data they shouldn't, from rogue agents breaching systems to banks scrambling to keep autonomous software out of sensitive accounts.

extraction.body: Would someone with real power in this country show some interest in national security? In Washington, Silicon Valley, Wall Street? Anyone out there? We're not picky. The world knows that Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy named Alice Huang. She's not related to Jensen. Alice was a top executive at Megaspeed, a chip buyer operating out of Singapore. U.S. investigators suspect the company is really a Chinese operation. Nvidia, the Silicon Valley maker of powerful semiconductors, is now one of the richest companies on the planet. The U.S. bans exports of its most advanced chips to China, which covets them in its race to build an AI industry bigger than America's. Alice's husband Kang Wei, a Chinese businessman who runs a China-backed data-center empire, introduced her to Jensen. Alice may very well bear responsibility for steering some of Nvidia's most powerful chips into China's hands. Investigators suspect that Megaspeed acted as the conduit. It took more than one clever guy in a cool black leather jacket to get away with this, or to think he could. It took a village of powerful interests that looked the other way because so much money was flowing their way. Who are the villagers? Start with Donald Trump, Jensen Huang's mighty defender. Jensen could have written in the manual on how to get even richer by flattering the U.S. president. He knew to pour millions into Trump vanity projects and to give him standing ovations. When Trump, at Jensen's prodding, unveiled a plan to send some fancy chips to Chinese customers, Jensen led the applause. And what about Nvidia's board of directors? Directors are supposed to oversee corporate governance. Jensen's hoo-ha with Alice was no secret. Pictures of the two together are all over social media. The best explanation for the board's looking the other way is that its members were making billions off business as usual. One director, Mark Stevens, has pocketed at least $2.7 billion selling Nvidia stock. Another, Tench Coxe, holds about $4.7 billion in Nvidia shares. Over at the Commerce Department, Secretary Howard Lutnick made sure Megaspeed didn't land on the government's trade blacklist. He did this after he'd been handed a Rubio memo warning about Megaspeed's dealings with China. Commerce also halted an investigation into Megaspeed over suspected AI chip smuggling to China. Apparently, all it took was an inquiry to Lutnick from Nvidia's general counsel. In the wake of this scandal, the Commerce Department has issued new rules tightening export controls on advanced chips to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil. Meanwhile, some highly paid Nvidia employees were so tone-deaf to Jensen Huang's apparent betrayal of American interests that they agitated to bring him back as CEO. And wouldn't you know it? Trump himself said that's not a bad idea. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America," Jensen said, "I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." Note how he tacked "America" onto the end of the list. The village that allowed this outrage to continue for so long is still intact. And chances are good that it still doesn't care.
